MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • Industry observers note that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and fresh Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

Industry observers note that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

According to recent reports, FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

It has been revealed that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each upcoming token goes through the model as a single row, so the substantial matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Recent findings suggest that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Industry observers note that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

According to recent reports, in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Recent findings suggest that the decoding kernel reveals up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

According to recent reports, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them latest paths through Metal:.

Sources indicate that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

According to recent reports, one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

Sources indicate that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

According to recent reports, work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Recent findings suggest that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

It has been revealed that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

According to recent reports, bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A massive thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

The Bank of Spain calculates that Spain alone faces a shortfall of about 750,000.

Rabobank anticipates that a large share of its clients will use the automated route, which should allow relationship managers to devote more time to supporting customers’ growth. nCino’s built-in AI and governance tools are expected to let the bank expand its use of AI across the whole lending process in a responsible way, with staff retaining authority over decisions and with transparency, auditability and oversight embedded throughout.

nCino serves more than 2,700 customers globally, ranging from community banks, credit unions and independent mortgage banks to some of the world’s biggest financial institutions. Its agentic platform is built specifically for financial services and other regulated sectors, pairing AI agents with human teams in a “dual workforce” model intended to remove inefficiencies, improve decision-making and produce better results for end customers.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (239 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Wavefront: Low-Rank Drafting with Parallel Causal Refinement for Speculative Decoding

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (239 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31638v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by letting a cheap drafter propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Parallel block drafters such as DFlash and P-EAGLE propose a whole block in one forward pass, but they lose the dependence between tokens in the block; DSpark restores part of it with a lightweight correction head that runs sequentially. Measuring DSpark, we find that this head overrides the base prediction on most slots, so the expensive base readout through the target's full lm_head mostly provides a seed. We therefore propose Wavefront, which follows a simple principle: shrink the base and strengthen the correction head. Wavefront replaces the full lm_head with a learned low-rank base, conditions the correction head on the whole drafted prefix within the same block, and resolves it with a few parallel Jacobi passes. A fixed pass budget makes the draft step free of data-dependent control flow, so we capture it as a single CUDA graph in vLLM with fused kernels. On Qwen3-8B, Wavefront improves throughput over xPress, DSpark and DFlash by 2.6%, 10.7% and 23.6% on average across math, code, chat and agentic benchmarks, and by 9.6%, 14.3% and 28.9% on SPEED-Bench long-context prompts. On Qwen3.8-27B it leads DFlash2, DSpark and xPress by 7.6%, 10.6% and 5.0%, and by 7.4%, 5.8% and 6.0% on the same long-context prompts. The gains persist as serving load grows to concurrency 32.

Web Search on Amazon Bedrock, the tool that grounds AI agents and applications in cited, current web information, now supports five fresh languages, plus non-US English, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Amazon Bedrock: Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Japanese. Agents serving customers in these languages get results that draw on local-language sources.

According to recent reports, we are also introducing a new optional country field that biases results toward sources from a specific country - just pass an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code, such as “JP” or “DE”. This is useful for agents that serve consumers in multiple countries, for questions whose answer depends on the user's actual or preferred location (e.g., local regulations, prices or public officials), and for surfacing regional sources.

Both the expanded language support and the optional  country field are available today in every Region where Web Search is offered: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland) for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and US Regions for Web Search on Amazon Bedrock. Queries are processed in the Region you call, helping organizations meet data residency requirements. Existing customers get the fresh language capabilities automatically, with no code changes, and pricing is the same in every language.

To get started with Web Search on Amazon Bedrock, checkout the developer guide and the web search product page.

Self-Improving Long-Horizon Reasoning by Learning Summaries from Local Continuations

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (246 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • It has been revealed that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

It has been revealed that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

Recent findings suggest that the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Sources indicate that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

It has been revealed that to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

It has been revealed that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Industry observers note that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Industry observers note that models too massive for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

It has been revealed that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

It has been revealed that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It has been revealed that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel aims. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Sources indicate that TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch consumers. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

In a recent development, we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

#36018. Industry News: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4193 w)

Industry News: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our GPT‑6 family of models can design newly introduced protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
  • An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks.
  • In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our GPT‑6 family of models can design newly introduced protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing latest proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Industry observers note that scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept latest kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Sources indicate that points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

It has been revealed that the models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

Industry observers note that the model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.

With our research partner, Onava⁠(opens in a new window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

According to recent reports, our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

Recent findings suggest that GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab.

We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study⁠(opens in a new window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.

An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target.

We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose upcoming ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

Recent findings suggest that for three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.

We also asked GPT‑6.2 to design new sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) highlighted binding.

Given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both revealed signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence.

Industry observers note that the unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

Sources indicate that researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called affinity maturation. They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design upcoming loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target.

We started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design new sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding to IL-4Rα.

We then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) demonstrated binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want.

Our model was asked to design small proteins with specified shapes: mainly coils (orange), mainly strands (blue), or a mix. Some instructions also specified how many coils or strands to include. The designs are intended to attach to PD-L1 or PD-1, shown in gray.

Most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a upcoming enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place.

We tested our models on 30 challenges from MotifBench⁠(opens in a new window), including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a motif, and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called motif scaffolding.

In a recent development, for each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and ESMFold⁠(opens in a latest window) to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed.

In a recent development, in a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities.

An internal research model designed protein structures around a small region whose shape had to stay fixed, shown in gold. The colored shapes compare the model’s designs with computer predictions of how the proteins would fold. Panels showing only gold had no design that passed the computer checks.

In motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from CATH⁠(opens in a latest window), a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space.

Recent findings suggest that many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them.

According to recent reports, we counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model.

Recent findings suggest that an internal research model was asked to design proteins with specified overall shapes, such as bundles of coils or layers of strands. The colored shapes compare selected designs with computer predictions of how they would fold, showing examples where the two closely match.

Many medicines, including aspirin, are small molecules, chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called docking. These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented.

In a recent development, for our first docking test, we used the PoseBusters dataset⁠(opens in a fresh window), a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model.

Sources indicate that in practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds. One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt. We tested this on 179 structures from the Scarpino dataset⁠(opens in a fresh window), where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in 92% of scored predictions⁠(opens in a new window), and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while DiffDock⁠(opens in a new window) reached 60%.

An internal research model predicted where and how small molecules would fit against proteins, shown in gray. Purple indicates the model’s predictions, and teal shows the molecules’ positions determined in earlier experiments. In these examples, the predictions closely match the experimental structures.

In a recent development, where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we highlighted the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces.

With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting.

Because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems.

Industry observers note that each row compares four models’ predictions of how an antibody attaches to its target protein. Colored shapes show the model’s prediction; dark gray shows the position observed in experiments. Results improved with each successive generation of model.

Sources indicate that we can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target.

It has been revealed that we drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only.

Sources indicate that in one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called rank correlation. A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model.

In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model.

Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called TM-score. A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold.

The biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone.

What if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone.

Each model was given the same protein sequence—the order of its chemical building blocks—and asked to predict its 3D shape. The colored shapes show the predictions, and dark gray shows the structure measured in experiments.

In a recent development, each model was given a partial structure and tasked with predicting the missing regions corresponding to the antibody CDRs. The colored regions show predictions from the internal model and ESMFold2 compared with the experimentally determined structures.

According to recent reports, it is important to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.

In a recent development, our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.

Industry observers note that some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.

According to recent reports, the laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.

Sources indicate that this work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.

Sources indicate that find minibinders for harder targets. We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.

Design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.

Sources indicate that design a wider range of molecules. Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.

As we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for fresh medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework⁠ guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.

According to recent reports, while lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of new biotechnologies and new medicines.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lassie, the Swedish pet health and insurance business, has struck a deal with MoneySuperMarket that makes the comparison platform the sole UK site where consumers can compare and purchase its prevention-focused pet cover for an initial three months.

The arrangement is designed to widen Lassie’s reach among UK pet owners. Through its app, policyholders can make a claim simply by taking a photo of their vet’s receipt, with the firm’s AI-driven process seeing upwards of 60% of claims worldwide wrapped up in roughly six minutes end to end. The same app also lets customers handle the day-to-day management of their policy.

Lassie entered the UK market in July and pairs insurance with tailored preventative care, aiming to support healthier pets through routine activities. Users receive weekly programmes shaped around their animal’s breed, age and life stage, covering areas such as nutrition, vaccinations, socialisation and training. The platform offers over 200 short courses alongside expert video content, and owners collect points for finishing health-related tasks. These points can then be converted into cheaper premiums, discounts and loyalty perks.

The InsurTech counts the owners of over 300,000 cats and dogs as customers across the UK, Sweden, Germany and France.

Sources indicate that moneySuperMarket director of insurance Sara Newell stated, “We’re always looking for upcoming ways to give our customers more choice and help them find pet insurance that works for them. Lassie brings something genuinely different to the market by combining cover with practical tools and rewards that help owners look after their pets. We’re pleased to make Lassie available through a UK price comparison site for the first time, making it easier for pet owners to compare their options and find the right cover.”.

It has been revealed that lassie CEO and co-founder Hedda Båverud Olsson noted, “Partnering with MoneySuperMarket puts Lassie in front of a far larger share of UK pet owners at the moment they’re looking for cover. We know that many pet health problems can be prevented, so we believe pet insurance should do more than pay claims once something has gone wrong. We built Lassie to help owners stay ahead of issues, using AI, behavioural science and gamification to make everyday pet care simpler and more rewarding. We’re delighted to bring this approach to MoneySuperMarket’s customers, helping them keep their pets healthier for longer and making it simple to claim when they need to.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • In a recent development, this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

In a recent development, this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

In a recent development, the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Newly introduced Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

Industry observers note that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

Sources indicate that the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Industry observers note that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table highlights that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

According to recent reports, the table demonstrates which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Sources indicate that each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Sources indicate that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Recent findings suggest that in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

In a recent development, with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

It has been revealed that the table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

It has been revealed that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

According to recent reports, key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Recent findings suggest that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

arXiv:2611.31611v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: Designing linear solvers for discretized partial differential equations requires problem-specific expertise. We present a multi-agent framework, in which language-model agents propose, critique, implement, and evaluate solver configurations assembled from Krylov methods, preconditioners, block factorizations, and neural operators. Inside the proposing agent, a non-dominated sorting genetic evolutionary algorithm evolves the population of meta-solvers toward the Pareto front of six measured quantities, so that one run returns a front of trade-offs rather than a single tuned solver. The system runs on small open-weight language models served on a single laptop, and we compare it with a single agent on four problems. For three-dimensional acoustic scattering and elasticity, it delivers 47 and 48 convergent hybrid solvers out of 60 candidates. Relative to the Jacobi-preconditioned Krylov baselines, the best of the discovered solvers reduce the iteration counts by factors of 4.7 and 60 and the online solve time by factors of 2.3 and 3.0, whereas the single agent produces no executable blueprint. For coupled dynamic thermoelasticity in two and three dimensions, where the baselines fail, it completes 98 of 100 transient candidates and, compared with the single agent, reaches a given accuracy 15 times faster in two dimensions and a displacement error 20 times lower in three dimensions.

The Stafford Building Society, a UK mutual lender, has deployed MV Shield, the financial crime compliance platform from Mutual Vision that runs on Napier AI technology.

The move brings the Society’s screening, monitoring and case management into a single system.

The rollout moves customer screening, transaction monitoring, customer risk assessment and know-your-customer (KYC) checks onto one unified platform.

Since the launch, initial signs show a drop in false positives, a lighter manual workload and quicker resolution of cases. Each decision is logged in a complete audit trail, which helps the Society prepare for audits and engage with regulators.

The Society chose MV Shield largely because it was built with mutuals in mind. It pairs Napier AI’s detection capabilities, which align with Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) expectations, with Mutual Vision’s experience of working with building societies for more than 25 years, along with locally based support.

Because screening, monitoring and case management sit together in a no-code environment, staff can assess alerts from one page and change rules and thresholds without outside help. They can also trial adjustments in a Sandbox before putting them into production, so they no longer need to raise tickets with the vendor.

MV Shield forms part of Mutual Vision’s updated technology offering for the mutual sector. It was created for the small compliance teams common at smaller societies. It gives them the kind of detection tools normally used by much larger organisations, in a format they can set up, test and manage on their own.

In a recent development, the Stafford Building Society CRO & MLRO Michelle Pledger mentioned, “We are a small team with the same risk exposure as a much bigger one. What sold us was control: screening, monitoring and workflow in one platform, and the ability to change rules and test them ourselves, the same day a risk emerges.”.

Recent findings suggest that napier AI CEO Greg Watson said, “Money laundering cost the UK economy £156.7bn ($206bn) last year and continues to rise, as found by the Napier AI / AML Index 26-27. That means the scale of the challenge of financial crime compliance teams is growing too.

“We are delighted to partner with Mutual Vision to bring best-in-class AML solutions to mutuals, with embedded AI that helps small teams tackle financial crime efficiently without compromising on compliance.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Luxembourg’s investment fund managers have until the end of the year to show the regulator exactly how they use artificial intelligence, and a single answer could determine how much scrutiny follows.
  • According to Zeidler Group, the latest joint survey from the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF) and the Banque centrale du Luxembourg (BCL) deserves far more attention than its statistical label suggests.
  • Released on 17 November 2026, the questionnaire must be submitted via eDesk by 31 December 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Luxembourg’s investment fund managers have until the end of the year to show the regulator exactly how they use artificial intelligence, and a single answer could determine how much scrutiny follows.

According to Zeidler Group, the latest joint survey from the Commission de Surveillance du Secteur Financier (CSSF) and the Banque centrale du Luxembourg (BCL) deserves far more attention than its statistical label suggests.

Released on 17 November 2026, the questionnaire must be submitted via eDesk by 31 December 2026. Authorised investment fund managers are among the addressees, alongside banks, investment firms, payment and e-money institutions, specialised and support PFS, crypto-asset service providers and Luxembourg branches.

Zeidler Group notes that while the exercise is framed as a survey, it hands the CSSF a detailed view of each manager’s AI usage, governance arrangements and dependence on third-party providers.

Sources indicate that this is the third AI survey run jointly by the two authorities. The first, held between October 2021 and January 2022, covered only credit, payment and e-money institutions. Fund managers were brought in for the second round in mid-2024, and the findings, published in May 2025, explain the regulator’s interest.

Investment fund managers made up the largest respondent group, at 261 of 461 participants. Roughly half were already using AI or planned to within a year, and they were the only category where most machine learning use cases (57%) depended on third-party vendor solutions. Across all respondents, only 43% had a formally approved AI policy.

According to recent reports, on eDesk, the procedure sits under “Investment funds and vehicles / Investment fund managers”. Zeidler Group highlights that this makes it particularly relevant for UCITS management companies authorised under Chapter 15 of the Law of 17 December 2010 and AIFMs authorised under Chapter 2 of the Law of 12 July 2013.

Industry observers note that there is some ambiguity over whether participation is optional. The CSSF communiqué states the questionnaire “must be completed and submitted” by the deadline, while the user guide calls participation voluntary but “strongly recommends” it. Zeidler Group advises managers to treat it as an expected submission, not least because a non-response will be visible to the supervisor.

It has been revealed that the questionnaire has five sections: General, Digital Strategy, AI technologies, AI third-party providers, and up to ten AI use cases. The pivotal point is question 6, where firms classify their most advanced AI use case as concrete (A), experimental or proof of concept (B), or not planned within 12 months (C). Only option C restricts the exercise to the first two sections.

It has been revealed that zeidler Group warns that AI is often more widespread than firms assume. Staff using GenAI tools such as ChatGPT or Copilot may already fall under options A or B, and AI deployed by delegated portfolio managers, central administrators or other service providers may also be relevant, both for the survey and for delegate oversight.

Firms should check their eDesk dashboard, align answers with their DORA register of information, outsourcing and delegation records and internal AI policies, and be ready to explain material changes since 2024. Conducting officers, IT, compliance and risk teams should agree responses before submission.

Zeidler Group also recommends using the exercise as a gap analysis, particularly around AI policies, rules on public GenAI tools and staff AI literacy, which has been required for deployers under Article 4 of the EU AI Act since 2 February 2025.

For more, read the full report here.
