💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.
  • Sources indicate that expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
  • It has been revealed that existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Sources indicate that expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

It has been revealed that existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

Sources indicate that in a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

In a recent development, left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

Recent findings suggest that this means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

According to recent reports, this effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective).

Industry observers note that when we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:.

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error.

It has been revealed that because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:.

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣.

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:.

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}.

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:.

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In a recent development, in terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more crucial. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub concerns autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrated that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

It has been revealed that this command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

In a recent development, to complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916.

Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (248 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AWS CodeDeploy can now suspend Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during EC2 in-place deployments to Auto Scaling groups.
  • In a recent development, you can choose to suspend any combination of these processes (Terminate, AZRebalance, InstanceRefresh, and ScheduledActions) on a deployment group, or on a single deployment.
  • You can configure this feature by using the CodeDeploy console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs.

Industry observers note that AWS CodeDeploy can now suspend Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during EC2 in-place deployments to Auto Scaling groups. CodeDeploy is a fully managed service that automates application deployments to Amazon EC2 instances, on-premises servers, AWS Lambda functions, and Amazon ECS services. This launch helps prevent scaling activities from terminating or replacing instances while CodeDeploy is updating them, which can cause a deployment to fail.

In a recent development, you can choose to suspend any combination of these processes (Terminate, AZRebalance, InstanceRefresh, and ScheduledActions) on a deployment group, or on a single deployment. CodeDeploy suspends the processes you choose before it deploys and resumes them when the deployment succeeds, fails, or is stopped, so you don't need custom scripts to suspend and resume processes during deployments. A setting on the deployment group applies to every deployment in that group, including deployments that your existing pipelines start.

You can configure this feature by using the CodeDeploy console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or AWS SDKs. This feature is available in all AWS Regions, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions.

To learn more, see Suspending Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling processes during deployments in the AWS CodeDeploy User Guide, or visit the AWS CodeDeploy product page.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31301v2 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/.

Decision Models in Hugging Face

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text.
  • Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.
  • Recent findings suggest that "I was charged twice for my subscription.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.

Recent findings suggest that "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.".

The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

This is the key idea behind decision models.

According to recent reports, A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

In a recent development, typeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models).

For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:.

Recent findings suggest that we could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

However, there are a few problems with this approach.

Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:.

A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

It has been revealed that zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

Recent findings suggest that one common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

Recent findings suggest that decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

Consider these three approaches:.

Sources indicate that the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

A decision model request has the following two components:.

The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:.

Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

Which department should handle this customer request?

The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

Industry observers note that the model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:.

pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​.

Here, KKK is the number of choices.

Consider this illustrative distribution:.

Industry observers note that ∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

The model chooses the option with the largest probability:.

y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​.

In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

Industry observers note that choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

How urgent is this customer request?

The model again produces a probability distribution:.

Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:.

E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​.

E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7.

The reported score is therefore 1.7.

Industry observers note that this does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

Is the customer requesting a refund?

Industry observers note that rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

Let YYY represent a binary outcome:.

Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p).

P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

According to recent reports, the model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

In a recent development, so far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

Industry observers note that the full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:.

pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​.

where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:.

C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997.

Sources indicate that notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

According to recent reports, decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

In a recent development, our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:.

The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

Recent findings suggest that transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:.

Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:.

Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:.

This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a upcoming model.

llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:.

The default server runs on port 9931.

According to recent reports, we can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

The useful property is interface compatibility.

Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

According to recent reports, once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

Recent findings suggest that below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it demonstrates the parts that matter:.

Recent findings suggest that first-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

Decision models are interesting not because classification is new, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

Sources indicate that traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

Industry observers note that great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that says whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator.

For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

"Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

According to recent reports, amazon Inspector has expanded its vulnerability management capabilities with runtime reachability analysis for findings originating from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances. Previously, Inspector reported every vulnerability found in a resource, including packages that were never used by applications. Security teams had to manually assess which vulnerabilities actually posed risk in their deployed environments. Now, Inspector automatically identifies which vulnerabilities are potentially reachable by analyzing package placement in container images and process activity on EC2 instances.

It has been revealed that with runtime reachability analysis, you can focus remediation efforts on vulnerabilities that matter most to your security posture. For container images, Inspector determines whether a vulnerable package is within your application's dockerfile paths defined by WORKDIR, ENTRYPOINT, or CMD instructions. For EC2 instances, Inspector identifies whether a vulnerable package was observed running as a process during the most recent scan. For EC2, customers must use the Inspector VM Scanner for agent-based scanning to get this capability. This helps organizations managing large container fleets or complex applications prioritize remediation by distinguishing between vulnerabilities that are potentially reachable versus those in unused dependencies, reducing noise and enabling development and security teams to work more efficiently. Newly generated findings will have runtime reachability analysis included, and backfill of existing findings will be completed over time.

Runtime reachability for Inspector findings is available at no additional charge and is available in all AWS Regions where Inspector is already available.

To learn more, visit the Amazon Inspector product page.

Irreducible Governance Structure for Autonomous Agent Systems: Fair Allocation, Strategy-Proofness, and Multi-Scale Composition

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (244 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31284v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Autonomous agent governance is commonly framed as a problem of enforcing correct execution. However, in multi-agent systems, an equally fundamental question precedes execution: which agents are allowed to act. In this paper, we show that allocation is not an auxiliary concern but a structural component of governance. When multiple agents compete for execution under constrained resources, any allocation mechanism introduces unavoidable trade-offs between fairness, efficiency, and resistance to strategic manipulation. We formalize this through a set of impossibility results, including Sybil amplification and the incompatibility of desirable allocation properties. We then show that these allocation constraints cannot be resolved within a single layer of control. Instead, they propagate across the system, interacting with execution atomicity, state enforcement, and behavioral drift. This leads to a multi-scale governance structure composed of four orthogonal dimensions: temporal (atomicity), state (enforcement), behavioral (drift monitoring), and population (allocation). Our main result is an irreducibility theorem: under finite observability, no governance architecture can collapse these dimensions without loss of correctness or stability. Allocation, in particular, acts as a first-class constraint that prevents simplification of the governance stack. We validate these results through a series of analytical constructions and empirical ablations, showing that removing or approximating any layer leads to systematic failure modes. This work reframes agent governance as a structural problem: not only how actions are executed, but how access to execution is determined, and why these decisions impose irreducible architectural requirements.

Breaking: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that more than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to newly introduced findings shared with WIRED.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that more than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to newly introduced findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.

Recent findings suggest that the findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.

Recent findings suggest that “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” notes Greg Pollock, the director of research at security firm UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”.

Sources indicate that the two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.

Exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more notable than ever to attackers.

The data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock notes.

It has been revealed that the China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He claims the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.

According to recent reports, pollock, who has investigated data privacy and breaches for many years, notes that he attempted to validate the data during the time it was accessible, but he can’t be certain about its fidelity or whether the same trove has been circulated elsewhere. It is also possible that it contains duplicate records, though Pollock attempted to check for this. He emphasizes that it seemed like the data had been analyzed carefully for maximum value to its owner.

In a recent development, “Someone had done some work to bring together a bunch of data and then normalize it to make it useful,” he states. “There’s no legitimate source on Earth that would have all of these things structured in this way, but if you had all of these breaches and brought them together, that would be valuable to an attacker.”.

The larger of the two exposed databases, found by longtime security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contained around 2 billion credentials and appeared to be data stolen by info-stealer malware, which can collect all login details being used on an infected machine, and collections of other data from potential cybercriminal activity. There is no indication that individual companies or institutions were breached to compile the data, Fowler says.

“After finding a couple of different repositories for info stealers and malware, I have a search signature to look for them,” Fowler explains to WIRED. “When this popped up, I could not believe just how big it was.”.

Fowler notes there were 8,471 folders in the exposed database containing plaintext credentials and account details. Some of the folders were named by country, including the US, UK, France, Germany, and dozens more. He found hundreds of millions of mainstream email accounts, tens of millions of .gov, .edu, and .org email addresses, more than 100 million social media accounts, and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.

It has been revealed that fowler could not determine who owned the database, but he contacted the hosting manufacturer, which removed it from the internet. It’s unclear how long it was online or if anyone else accessed the information.

The enormous scale of the two exposures could create a sense of hopelessness that individuals are powerless to defend their private information. And there is a public understanding about the extent of data theft across the web. But both researchers point out that after years of this escalating situation, protections like using password managers and enabling multi-factor authentication really have broadly proved effective at keeping attackers out of consumer accounts, even if they aren’t silver bullets against every kind of attack.

Industry News: Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
  • Sources indicate that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
  • In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up promptly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Sources indicate that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

In a recent development, this post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Recent findings suggest that pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

In a recent development, A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

Industry observers note that the useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

Industry observers note that hierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

It has been revealed that these merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:.

With pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

Sources indicate that this distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Sources indicate that pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

Industry observers note that cachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

In a recent development, the poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

In a recent development, the script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Industry observers note that sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Recent findings suggest that let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

According to recent reports, you can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

According to recent reports, I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

It has been revealed that for adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

Sources indicate that at the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

Sources indicate that the gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

Industry observers note that if the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

Sources indicate that multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

Amazon SageMaker Studio now provides a native developer experience for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, enabling data scientists to submit distributed training jobs, deploy models, and monitor workloads through a visual interface on HyperPod clusters orchestrated with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). SageMaker HyperPod is a purpose-built infrastructure for distributed training and fine-tuning of foundation models at scale, designed to reduce infrastructure management overhead. Submitting training jobs and deploying custom models on HyperPod at scale requires familiarity with kubectl and authoring Kubernetes manifests, creating operational burden for data scientists who prefer to work in an interactive development environment.

Recent findings suggest that with this launch, data scientists can now submit distributed PyTorch and Ray training jobs and deploy models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, Amazon S3, or Amazon FSx, through single-page forms with a live YAML preview in SageMaker Studio. Compute configurations in the forms provide reusable resource presets that data scientists select when submitting training jobs or deploying models, eliminating manual compute entry. Metrics and logs are embedded directly in the detail pages, powered by HyperPod Observability and Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, surfacing Kubernetes conditions and events, CloudWatch logs, and embedded metrics so data scientists can diagnose workloads without leaving their environment. For teams managing multiple workloads and using HyperPod task governance, Studio provides a unified queue view where people can see all pending tasks across training jobs and inference services, and adjust a task's priority class directly to optimize cluster utilization.

These updates are available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Amazon EKS, in all AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker HyperPod and Amazon SageMaker Studio are currently supported.

To learn more, visit the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod in Studio documentation.

Latest Update: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time.
  • Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment.
  • Recent findings suggest that building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

Recent findings suggest that building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives.

Sources indicate that botPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

It has been revealed that we first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

Recent findings suggest that finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

Recent findings suggest that the second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

In a recent development, each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Industry observers note that table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

It has been revealed that tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Sources indicate that table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Industry observers note that the largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

Recent findings suggest that botPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Sources indicate that simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

In a recent development, on complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

According to recent reports, complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

BotPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Recent findings suggest that shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Recent findings suggest that fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

Recent findings suggest that botPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

[3] Qian, Cheng, et al. "ToolRL: Reward is All Tool Learning Needs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025).

📖 0% read

Sources indicate that amazon Aurora serverless now supports database capacity of up to 384 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs) for Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, a 50% increase from the previous maximum of 256 ACUs. Each ACU provides approximately 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory with corresponding CPU and networking, so a single Aurora serverless database can now scale up to 768 GiB of memory. When the workload completes, Aurora serverless automatically scales down to zero. This makes Aurora serverless especially well-suited for agentic AI applications, which typically have bursts of activity, long idle windows, and unpredictable traffic patterns. Aurora serverless handles all of it automatically, scaling capacity with your agents, so you only pay for what you use. With 384 ACU support, customers can now use Aurora serverless for even more demanding workloads while continuing to scale down to zero when not in use, paying only for the capacity consumed. For newly introduced clusters, select a supported Aurora MySQL engine version and set your maximum capacity up to 384 ACUs. For existing clusters on Platform Version 4, simply modify the cluster to upgrade the maximum capacity setting (and the engine version if needed). There will be no downtime if your database is already on Platform Version 4. For existing clusters on older platform versions, upgrade to Platform Version 4 through a pending maintenance action. 384 ACU support is available for Aurora MySQL versions 3.14 and 8.4.10, running on Platform Version 4. To learn more, see Aurora serverless capacity in the Amazon Aurora User Guide. For pricing details and Region availability, visit Amazon Aurora Pricing. To get started, create or modify an Aurora serverless database in the AWS Management Console.
